wa_news_nw_corner.name: Northwest Corner (Boving-Pollack Route)
wa_news_nw_corner.fa: Paul Boving and Steve Pollack, September 25, 1976
gear: Extra-long slings/alpine draws for the leftward-traversing pitches
60-70m rope (needed if descending via the bolted West Face rappel line)
hazards: The route includes wide flake and offwidth pitches that require big gear; running low on large cams is a real risk.
Long, sometimes traversing pitches create rope drag that must be managed with long runners.

The Early Winters Spires are a serious alpine setting: on May 10, 2025, three climbers died and a fourth was seriously injured when a single old, rusted piton anchor pulled out while multiple people were clipped to it and rappelling in the Early Winter Couloir, the gully separating North and South Early Winters Spire (a different line than this route's own NW Corner descent gully). It's a hard reminder never to trust an old fixed pin without backup and never to load one anchor point with an entire party.
wa_news_nw_corner.overview: Northwest Corner (Boving-Pollack), 5.9+ III, is the classic moderate outing on North Early Winters Spire, the northern/lower of the two Early Winters Spires in the Liberty Bell Group at Washington Pass. First climbed by Paul Boving and Steve Pollack on September 25, 1976, it follows a corner system, the well-known 'Zig-Zag Flakes' pitch, and a burly offwidth up the peak's northwest aspect in 4-5 pitches (roughly 500 ft of climbing), finishing with a 4th-class traverse around a roof to the summit. It's one of the most popular moderate alpine rock routes at Washington Pass alongside the Beckey Route on Liberty Bell and the South Arete on South Early Winters Spire.
wa_news_nw_corner.beta: The Northwest Corner is a well-established four-to-five pitch route that ascends the natural corner system on the northwest aspect of North Early Winters Spire. This is one of the most popular routes on the peak, known for reliable rock quality and manageable protection requirements. The route follows a clear line with sustained climbing throughout.
wa_news_nw_corner.turnaround: Top out before afternoon thunderstorms; the spire summit is highly exposed.
wa_news_nw_corner.rappels: Two lines: the bolted West Face (six bolted stations), all single-rope on a 60 m rope that just barely reaches - a 70 m is the comfortable choice - or the classic line (3 single-rope raps to the notch, then a largely free-hanging double-rope rappel past the chockstone, then a short tree rap)
wa_news_nw_corner.permit: No climbing permit required; a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass, or day-use fee (Digital Day Pass / Scan & Pay) is needed for trailhead parking.
wa_news_nw_corner.comms: Cell phone coverage is unreliable on the route and summit; Verizon generally provides the best coverage among carriers. Coverage at the trailhead is variable. Satellite communication device (satellite phone or personal locator beacon) recommended for emergencies in this remote alpine location.
wa_news_nw_corner.descent: Follow the standard spire descent off the back side.
obj_haz: loose rock in trees on P1-P2

waypoints.name: Blue Lake Trailhead
waypoints.directions: From Winthrop, drive SR-20 west about 30 miles, over Washington Pass, to the signed Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of the highway about a mile west of the pass, at roughly 5,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or day-use fee is required to park. SR-20 is gated over Washington Pass through the winter, so there is no drive-up access until it reopens in spring.

waypoints.name: North Early Winters Spire
waypoints.directions: Follow the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to the signed climbing-access junction just past a small stream (the last water), then take the climbers' path up slabs, talus and heather into the basin under the west faces and traverse north along the base to a corner and crack leading to a treed ledge. Five pitches of 5.8-5.9 corners, wide cracks and an offwidth finish left around a roof to the summit.

wa_news_nw_corner.detailed_rack: Doubles 0.75"-3" (BD sizes 2-4), a single 4" (#5) piece, and singles from fingers to 1" cover the lower corner pitches; the P4 offwidth wants the #4-5 pieces though the climbing is more secure than it looks via face-smears/arm-bars even where gear is sparse. Carry several extra-long slings for P2, P3, and the P5 roof traverse to control rope drag. A 60m rope is the minimum for the bolted West Face rappel descent.
pro_tips: Carry a few extra long slings to extend belays on P2, P3, and the P5 roof traverse and cut rope drag
If descending the classic gully, inspect any fixed piton before weighting it and back it up with your own gear
Prefer the newer 6-station bolted rappel line down the West Face when rope length and conditions allow — cleaner and faster than the loose gully
A 70m rope is more comfortable than 60m if you plan to descend via the bolted rap line
On P2, stay left/on-line off the belay ledge — parties have accidentally wandered right onto the adjacent West Face route here.
watch_out: Inspect any fixed piton before weighting it on the descent and back it up with your own gear (cam, picket, or nut) — see the 2025 anchor-failure fatality on this peak's east-side gully
Stay left on P2 to avoid drifting onto the neighboring West Face route
P4's offwidth and P5's slab both get noticeably harder/wetter in early season or after rain given the NW aspect
Start early to be off the summit before typical PNW afternoon thunderstorm buildup
wa_news_nw_corner.pro_needs: Standard alpine trad rack to #4 Camalot with doubles in the 2-4" range, plus a single #5; a 60m (70m more comfortable) rope if descending via the bolted rappel line.
wa_news_nw_corner.best_season: Prime conditions are typically August into September once the north-facing rock has dried out; the route can still hold snow and wet rock into late June/early July given its NW aspect, especially after a big winter. Check NWAC's Washington Pass zone and recent trip reports for approach/gully snow before an early-season attempt.
wa_news_nw_corner.approach: Start at the Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of Hwy 20 (elev. ~5,400 ft), about one mile west of the Washington Pass Overlook and roughly 30 miles west of Winthrop. Follow the well-graded Blue Lake Trail southwest through subalpine forest. At about 1.4-1.5 miles, watch for a signed junction: the main trail continues straight toward Blue Lake, while a climber's path splits left/south, signed for "Liberty Bell Trail #727 – Climbing Access," reached just past a small stream/meadow that is the last reliable water source before the basin. Take the climber's trail, which switchbacks up through slabs, talus, and heather meadows into the Liberty Bell/Early Winters basin beneath the west faces of the spire group — roughly another 0.5 mile and 1,000-1,300 ft of gain, putting total approach distance at about 2 miles with 1,300-1,600 ft of gain from the car (most parties report 1-2 hours). From the upper basin, continue scrambling/traversing north along the base of North Early Winters Spire's west side to a distinctive corner/crack system that leads to a tree-covered ledge — the shared start for the Northwest Corner and West Face. Hazards: lingering snow and occasional avalanche debris in the basin and approach gully well into June (many early-season parties boot or ski the lower approach), talus and slab sections with some route-finding among braided climbers' paths, and no dependable water once past the stream near the Liberty Bell Trail junction, so fill up there.
wa_news_nw_corner.descent_text:
Two established ways off the summit; both are widely used and either works, but they return you to different spots relative to a gear stash at the base.

Bolted West Face rappel line (most direct back to packs at the base of NW Corner/West Face): from the summit, downclimb/walk skier's-left to the top of a clean, purpose-bolted rappel line down the right side of the West Face. Six bolted (2-bolt) rappel stations in a nearly direct line bring you back down to essentially the same spot where you left your pack at the base of the route. Pulls are reported as clean and the line is efficient — regulars find it a breeze. A single 60m rope is just barely sufficient (one station, reportedly the 3rd rappel, is tight enough that you may need to reach down to clip your PAS/daisy to the anchor and feed rope through your device to reach it); a 70m rope removes that squeeze and is the more comfortable choice. No natural anchors needed on this line — it's fully bolted.

Classic notch/chockstone descent (South/Southwest Gully): downclimb and rappel the south side into the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire, then continue down the Southwest Gully (the South Early Winter Spire "Chockstone Route" descent). This runs three single-rope rappels from near the summit down to the notch/gully (which often holds snow even in summer), followed by one spectacular, largely free-hanging double-rope rappel down and past a huge chockstone (~50 ft of air), then a final short rappel (~30 ft, off a tree anchor) or downclimb/scramble to reach the base. Total is about 4-5 rappels on this line. Anchors are natural/fixed slings around the chockstone and trees rather than bolts — inspect webbing before trusting it. Summit-to-base time on this descent is typically around 1.5-2 hours. This option is the standard descent if you climbed a route on the south/southwest side, or as a backup if the West Face bolt line is congested or iced.
wa_news_nw_corner.bail: Belay ledges allow retreat, but the wide pitches make lowering/rappelling awkward; plan gear accordingly.

pitch_detail.belay: Belay on the broad, tree-covered ledge reached after the crack, corner and short chimney.
pitch_detail.notes: 45m crack/corner topped by a short, poorly protected chimney section; easy climbing gains a broad, tree-covered ledge used as the first belay.
50m up and left, weaving through trees (and often lingering snow patches) and a corner to reach a second belay ledge; sustained but moderate climbing.
30m up a left-leading flake and wide crack requiring big cams (bring the #4-#5!); committing 5.9 liebacks lead to a belay slung around a small rock pillar.
25m of surprisingly secure offwidth: smear the face while arm-barring the crack for balance. Widely cited as the burly technical crux, ending at a sloping ledge below a roof.
30m traverse left around the roof (watch rope drag), then easing cracks lead directly to the summit; low 4th class scrambling to finish.

itinerary.cal: Route is dry-season rock only; plan for a June-September window.

days.note: This is a standard single-day alpine rock outing out of Washington Pass, not an overnight trip. Parties hike the Blue Lake Trail and climber's path into the basin below the Liberty Bell group, scramble to the base, climb 4-5 pitches of sustained 5.8-5.9 up the corner/dihedral system, then descend via a bolted rappel line straight back to the packs.

schedule.label: Leave Blue Lake trailhead

schedule.label: Reach base of route
schedule.detail: ~1.5 mi on the Blue Lake Trail, then the well-worn climber's trail into the basin and a short scramble to the start.

schedule.label: Start climbing (P1, 5.8 corner)
schedule.detail: 5 pitches, mostly sustained 5.9 with a burly 3-4" crack higher up; some parties link to 4 pitches.

schedule.label: Top out
schedule.detail: ~3.5 hrs of climbing for a fit, competent party.

schedule.label: Begin bolted rappels down the West Face

climate.fall: Good into September if the rock has fully dried.
climate.spring: Can still hold snow on the approach into June; some parties ski the approach in early season.
climate.summer: Best window, though still slower to dry after rain than south/west aspects.
climate.typical: Dry, sunny alpine summers are typical July-September with cool nights; the NW-facing rock on this route holds snow and stays damp later into the season than south-facing Washington Pass routes nearby.

bySeason.fall: Can be dry and cool with larch color by late Sept-Oct, but shortening days and early-season snow are a risk.
bySeason.spring: Approach and gully are often still snow-covered into June/July; expect boot- or ski-track approaches and wet rock on this NW aspect.
bySeason.summer: Best window (especially Aug-Sep); watch for typical PNW afternoon thunderstorm buildup.
bySeason.winter: Highway 20 is gated and the area is inaccessible.

crowds.peakTraffic: Weekends in July-August, the peak of the Washington Pass rock season
crowds.estimatePerSeason: No published route-specific count found; estimated roughly 20-40 parties per season given Washington Pass is one of the most-visited North Cascades rock climbing areas, tempered by the route's offwidth pitch and big-gear requirement which filter out less experienced/prepared parties compared to easier Washington Pass classics

fitnessSpec.hiking: Moderate approach hike/scramble from the Blue Lake trailhead area on Hwy 20, roughly 2-3 miles with meaningful elevation gain on climber's-trail terrain
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light single-day rack + rope + layers (roughly 15-25 lb); no glacier or overnight gear needed

partner_requirements.approachTime: Roughly 1.5-2.5 hours from the highway pullout to the base of the route
requiredSkills: offwidth/wide-crack technique (or willingness to grovel through the wide Pitch 4 section) plus enough big cams to protect it
multi-pitch rope management on long, traversing pitches to avoid drag
building and, critically, inspecting/backing up rappel anchors for the descent
basic alpine route-finding on an unmarked, featured granite face
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Solid alpine rock leader with prior multi-pitch trad experience; comfortable leading sustained 5.9/5.9+ granite well above gear and managing rope drag on traversing pitches. Not a suitable first alpine rock route.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late June through September, with July-August offering the most consistently dry rock and stable weather

July.reason: Prime Washington Pass season - warm, generally dry granite, and the most reliable stretch of stable high-pressure weather

June.reason: Only the tail end of June is typically in season; earlier in the month lingering snow patches on the approach and wet/cold rock are common before the route reliably comes into condition

August.reason: Continues to be prime season with dry rock, though this is also peak crowd season and can bring hot easterly heat waves

September.reason: Still climbable with cooling, often stable weather, but shorter daylight and an increasing chance of an early-season storm system moving in toward month's end

weather.typical: Typical North Cascades summer alpine pattern - clear, cool mornings with rock that can be slow to dry after a wet spell; the east-side Washington Pass microclimate is drier and can run hot in July-August compared to the west slopes
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms/build-ups are the main risk, most common in July and August

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Serious, sustained multi-pitch alpine exposure on 5.9+ terrain with committing traversing sections that create rope drag if not managed. The highest-consequence part of the route is the rappel descent, not the climbing itself: a May 2025 accident in which a rappel anchor failed on the North Spire and killed three climbers is a direct reminder to inspect and back up all rappel anchors rather than trusting fixed tat.

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer rock route; the approach falls within NWAC's East Slopes North forecast zone in winter/spring, but that has no bearing on the Late June-September climbing window

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: Drive SR 20 about 42 miles east from Newhalem, or about 31 miles west from Winthrop, to the Blue Lake trailhead on the south side of the highway just below Washington Pass; SR 20 is closed in winter.

rappel_detail.notes: First of three single-rope rappels down the south side toward the notch. Plan on near the full reach of a doubled 60 m rope.
hazards: committing to the wrong descent is the easy mistake here - the bolted West Face rappels start well away from this line
rappel_detail.station: This is the classic line, not the bolted West Face one, and the two leave the summit from different places. Scramble down south and west of the summit, then down and skier's left toward the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire; the first fixed station is on that side.

rappel_detail.notes: Second single-rope rappel continuing toward the notch/gully.
Third single-rope rappel reaching the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire.
hazards: the notch is often still snow-covered in summer - expect a wet or snowy stance and possibly a footwear change at the anchor
rappel_detail.station: This rappel lands in the notch and Southwest Couloir between North and South Early Winters Spire.

rappel_detail.pull: Described as a double-rope rappel; check the pull before the second climber commits, since there is no way back up to the anchor once you are hanging free.
rappel_detail.notes: Largely free-hanging double-rope rappel past a huge chockstone (~50 ft/15m of air). Plan on a typical double-rope pitch.
hazards: free-hanging and spinning below the chockstone
the anchor is webbing around a natural feature rather than hardware - inspect it and replace or back it up
rappel_detail.station: Fixed slings on the large chockstone blocking the couloir. The rappel goes off and past the chockstone and is largely free-hanging, about 50 ft of air.

rappel_detail.notes: Final short (~30 ft) rappel, or downclimb/scramble alternative, reaching the base of the Southwest Gully.
rappel_detail.station: Short rappel of about 30 ft off a tree at the bottom of the couloir; scrambling and downclimbing is the accepted alternative if the tree or its slings look poor.

wa_news_nw_corner.rappel_count_note: Two established descents. The bolted West Face line is six bolted single-rope stations; a 60 m rope only just reaches and a 70 m is the comfortable choice. The classic line is three single-rope rappels to the notch, a free-hanging double-rope rappel past the chockstone, then a short tree rappel or a downclimb to the ground; the table below lists the classic line.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail, then north along the base of the west side
approach_variants.notes:
Nearly all the routes on North Early Winters Spire are on its west side, so the Blue Lake Trailhead is the right side of the mountain to start from — the hairpin pullout on the east serves the East Buttress and couloir lines, not this one.

From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 about a mile west of Washington Pass, follow the maintained trail for roughly a mile and a half to the signed Liberty Bell Trail #727 climbing-access junction, which sits just past a small stream and is marked with a large cairn. That stream is your last reliable water.

Trail #727 switchbacks up slabs, talus and heather into the basin under the west faces. Approach as if for South Early Winters Spire and then traverse left (north) along the base of the formations, scrambling, until you are under North Early Winters Spire. Most parties report one to two hours from the car.
hazards: lingering snow and avalanche debris in the basin and approach gully into June
braided climbers' paths through the upper talus make it easy to drift onto the wrong formation
no water past the stream at the Trail #727 junction
poorly protected chimney section low on the first pitch
approach_variants.baseFinding: Keep traversing north along the base. The Northwest Corner begins at a distinct corner-and-crack system whose first pitch — around 45 metres of 5.8, including a short chimney section with sparse gear — runs up to a broad ledge covered in trees. That treed ledge is the landmark: it is visible from below and from across the basin, it is the top of pitch one, and the route continues up and left off its left-hand edge. If you are under blank slab with no corner leading to a treed ledge, you have not gone far enough north yet. The corner start is shared with the West Face route, so being at the right corner puts you at the right place for either — the two diverge above the ledge, not below it.

bivy.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside bivy
bivy.notes: The usual answer for a car-to-car day on this group, and the start of every west-side approach, about a mile west of Washington Pass. Parties routinely sleep at the lot or at the highway hairpin rather than walking in, because the approaches are short enough that a high camp buys little. There are no facilities and no water; it is a place to sleep in or beside the car, not a campsite. Highway 20 is closed through the winter, so this is unavailable until the road reopens.
bivy.water: None at the trailhead. Carry what you need.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park
bivy.capacity: Informal, at the parking area — no prepared sites

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground, about a ten-minute drive east down the highway from the Blue Lake trailhead, in the trees along Early Winters Creek. No reservations, so it is a gamble on a summer weekend. Its season runs roughly from late spring into autumn and is decided by snow rather than by a date.
bivy.water: Early Winters Creek runs through the campground

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground
bivy.notes: Further east and lower than Lone Fir, which means it opens earlier in the season when the higher options are still under snow — the practical choice for an early-season trip. It sits far enough off the highway to be quiet and has more plumbing than anything nearer the climbing. The trade is a longer drive to the trailhead each morning. Check current status before relying on it; the highway-corridor campgrounds take periodic maintenance closures.
bivy.water: Piped water, sinks and flush toilets

bivy.name: Liberty Bell basin dispersed sites
bivy.notes: Sites in the basin on the west side of the group, reached by following the Blue Lake trail and then the signed climbers' path that branches off it toward the group. Worth it if you want to be under the west-side routes at first light rather than walking up from the road. Note the separate restriction around Blue Lake itself, where overnight camping is not allowed within a quarter mile of the lake — the basin sites are the ones to aim for, not the lakeshore. Treat it as a basin camp below the spires rather than a fixed spot.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and seasonal runoff in the basin — unreliable once the snow has gone
bivy.permit: No permit for dispersed camping; this is national forest, not the national park

wa_north_early_winters_spire_northwest_c.name: Northwest Corner (a.k.a. Boving-Pollack Route)
wa_north_early_winters_spire_northwest_c.overview: Five pitches. P1 (5.8, 45 m): the corner-crack above the northward path along the base of the peak, to a treed ledge. P2 (5.9, 50 m): leftward through trees and a corner. P3 (5.9, 30 m): left-slanting flake and wide crack to a ledge with slings on a small pillar; keep the big gear for P4 (5.9, 25 m), an offwidth best handled by smearing the face with the right arm in the crack. P5 (4th class, 30 m): traverse left around the roof, mind the rope drag, then cracks to the summit. Six rappels down the west wall, one 70 m rope.
wa_north_early_winters_spire_northwest_c.detailed_rack: Cams and nuts up to 4-5 in.; carry long slings because the lengthy, wandering pitches drag the rope.

itinerary.cal: Summer to early fall, once the west-side gullies at Washington Pass are melted out.

days.note: Hike the Blue Lake Trail through its switchbacks for about two miles, then take the marked climbers' trail left to the foot of the Early Winter Spires and traverse north along the base of the north spire to the corner. Climb five pitches: a 5.8 corner with a short chimney, a 5.9 corner through trees, a 5.9 flake, the 5.9 offwidth that protects better than it looks, and a 4th-class traverse around the roof to the 7,760 ft top. Descend from the chains at the south end of the west face, making about six rappels on a single 70 m rope, including one free hang off a chockstone, then reverse the approach.
days.title: Blue Lake trailhead to the summit and back

schedule.label: Blue Lake trailhead
schedule.detail: The climbers' trail branches left after about two miles.

schedule.label: Base of the route
schedule.detail: About 2.5 miles and 1,900 ft from the car.

schedule.label: Back at the base
schedule.detail: Climb and rappels, base to base, for a competent party.

days.objective: Climb the Northwest Corner to the summit of North Early Winter Spire and rappel the west face

itinerary.totalNote: A single day from the Blue Lake trailhead: a short climbers' trail to the west face, five pitches of 5.8 to 5.9+ cracks (including an offwidth), then rappels down the west face and the walk back.

wa_south_early_winter_spire_direct_east_.name: Direct East Buttress
gear: double set of cams, green Alien to #3 Camalot
optional third set of finger-sized cams
hazards: sustained hard crack and face pitches
high exposure
afternoon thunderstorms
wa_south_early_winter_spire_direct_east_.overview: The direct version of South Early Winter Spire's classic East Buttress, climbing harder, steeper pitches low on the buttress before joining the upper line. A sustained, high-quality alpine rock route on excellent Washington Pass granite.
wa_south_early_winter_spire_direct_east_.beta: Ascend the prominent East Buttress via mixed rock and bolt-ladder terrain. Route is largely 5.8-5.9 with two crux pitches of 5.11 and one 5.10 connector. Bolt ladders on pitches 4 and 6 allow grade flexibility; many parties now free-climb the route entirely at 5.11.
wa_south_early_winter_spire_direct_east_.turnaround: Turn around if storms build over the Pass in the afternoon.
wa_south_early_winter_spire_direct_east_.rappels: 3 single-rope rappels on a 60 m rope from bolted chain anchors on the South Arete descent, each under 30 m, with easy downclimbing between them
wa_south_early_winter_spire_direct_east_.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit required; Northwest Forest Pass (or day fee) to park at developed trailheads.
wa_south_early_winter_spire_direct_east_.comms: No cell service at Washington Pass.
wa_south_early_winter_spire_direct_east_.descent: Descend the South Early Winter Spire descent gully/rappels back toward the Blue Lake approach.

waypoints.name: Hairpin Turn Pullout (Hwy 20)
waypoints.note: Dirt pullout at the hairpin switchback ~0.5-1mi east of Washington Pass, directly beneath the east faces of North/South Early Winters Spire; hike up Spire Gully to the NEWS-SEWS notch, then traverse left to the route base. Parties often descend via South Arete/Blue Lake Trail and hitchhike back to a car left here.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 to Washington Pass (the highway is closed over the pass in winter), then continue east, downhill, to the big hairpin switchback just below the pass; from the Mazama side it is the hairpin you reach as the road climbs to the pass. Park in the dirt pullout at the hairpin, about 5,100 ft, directly below the east faces of the Early Winters Spires. This is not the Blue Lake Trailhead.

waypoints.name: South Early Winters Spire
waypoints.directions: Hike up Spire Gully, following occasional cairns, to the last large tree in the middle of the gully, then traverse right across talus (snow early in the season) until you are under the gully that climbs to the North–South Early Winters Spires notch. Traverse left to the foot of the east buttress and climb its nine pitches to the summit.

sectionBreakdown.note: A sustained 9-pitch line (5.11 free, or 5.9 A0) to the summit. Descend by downclimbing the South Arete to the first bolted station, then 3 short s…

wa_south_early_winter_spire_direct_east_.detailed_rack: Double rack of small to medium cams, a set of nuts, and extra small pieces for the thin crux pitches.
pro_tips: The direct pitches are the crux — be solid at the grade before committing.
Start early to beat afternoon thunderstorms.
Carry small protection for the thin sections.
wa_south_early_winter_spire_direct_east_.pro_needs: Emphasis on small-to-medium protection for the sustained, harder direct pitches.
wa_south_early_winter_spire_direct_east_.best_season: Summer into early fall for dry, warm granite.
wa_south_early_winter_spire_direct_east_.approach: Park at the 'hairpin' pullout on Highway 20 (separate from the Blue Lake Trailhead), hike up Spire Gully following occasional cairns to the last large tree in the gully, then traverse right across talus (or snow early-season — bring crampons/axe) to the gully leading to the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire, then traverse left to the base of the east buttress. Roughly 1.5 hours car-to-base at a moderate pace; the line is visible from the road.
wa_south_early_winter_spire_direct_east_.descent_text: Downclimb the South Arete from the summit — mostly 3rd/4th class with one short, more exposed 5th-class section — down to bolted anchors above the standard SEWS descent gully, then make 3 single-rope rappels (60m rope) from bolted anchors/chains to the base of the wall. From the base, hike out via the climber's trail to the Blue Lake Trail; if you parked at the hairpin rather than the Blue Lake Trailhead, plan a short road walk or car shuttle back.
wa_south_early_winter_spire_direct_east_.bail: Rappel the route or traverse to the standard East Buttress to escape; the direct lower pitches are committing.

pitch_detail.belay: The belay is at the first sensible tree partway up the gully.
pitch_detail.notes: A rambling, typical alpine first pitch through moss, some loose rock, and vegetation to a tree anchor partway up the gully.

pitch_detail.belay: The belay is at the obvious tree at the end of the crack system.
pitch_detail.notes: A crack system winds through ledges past some loose 'kitty litter' rock to the base of the route's large dihedral.

pitch_detail.belay: The belay is on a ledge holding several trees, about sixty feet above the roof crux.
pitch_detail.notes: Climbs the dihedral through a bulging roof; the crux move is protected right at your waist by a good #4 cam before easier climbing ambles 60 ft to a tree ledge.

pitch_detail.belay: The belay is a hanging stance on two chained bolts at the top of the bolt ladder, very exposed.
pitch_detail.notes: The route's technical crux: 20 ft of 5.8/9 leads into a ladder of roughly 14 closely-spaced bolts (5.10+/A0), finishing with face moves and a finger crack; free climbers link it around 5.11a. Hanging belay off two bolts with chains.

pitch_detail.belay: The belay is on a small ledge at the top of the finger crack.
pitch_detail.notes: Traverse right clipping bolts to a beautiful finger crack that takes solid jams and gear, easing to 5.7 near the belay.

pitch_detail.belay: The belay is on a bolted ledge above the second bolt ladder.
pitch_detail.notes: A right-leaning crack with sketchy gear gives way to a second bolt ladder with two mandatory 5.9+ free mantle moves (aid at A0); ends at a bolted belay.

pitch_detail.belay: The belay is at a tree, after the wandering crack system above the ledge.
pitch_detail.notes: One hard move pulling off the belay ledge, then a wandering, well-featured crack system with sparse gear to a tree anchor.

Rambling ledges, cracks, and trees lead to a big ledge; skip the mossy slab above by trending left on a ramp to a final unprotected easy slab at a bolted anchor right on the east face's edge -- a spectacular, exposed top-out.
An exposed step-down off the last anchor onto a small ramp leads to easy terrain and the true summit; most parties simul-climb or solo this short finish.

days.note: A sustained 9-pitch line (5.11 free, or 5.9 A0) to the summit. Descend by downclimbing the South Arete to the first bolted station, then 3 short station-to-station rappels down the South Arete.
days.title: Car-to-car climb

schedule.label: Begin descent
schedule.detail: Downclimb 2 pitches, then 3 short rappels station-to-station.

days.objective: Climb the Direct East Buttress and return to the car

itinerary.totalNote: A long day: roughly 10.5 hrs car-to-car for 9 pitches up to 5.9-5.11/A0.

wa_south_early_winter_spire_direct_east_.corrections: 2026-08-01: access.rules corrected — the 1/4-mile no-camping buffer was misattributed to Cutthroat Lake instead of Blue Lake, the trailhead this route actually uses (same mixup pattern found on the neighboring Liberty Bell/Lexington Tower cluster in batches 18 and 40).

rappel_detail.pull: Built for a single 60 m rope, and the stations were placed to give steep, clean pulls clear of the gully.
rappel_detail.notes: First of three fixed rappel stations equipped in recent years on the South Arete; single 60m rope is sufficient for each rap.
rappel_detail.anchor: fixed bolt/chain station, climber's right of the summer gully/chimney
hazards: One party found one of these bolted stations placed on a large block that is not attached to the mountain: counted from the bottom it is the third, which with three stations in place is this top one, above the gully. Inspect the rock the bolts are in, not only the hardware, and back it up if you are not satisfied.
The short 5th-class step above the station is exposed with real fall consequence. Stay roped, and place gear on it rather than soloing down.
rappel_detail.station: Top station of the rappel line North Cascade Mountain Guides installed after the June 2022 rockfall: bolts and chains on a big ledge immediately above the small tree that older parties used to sling. All three new stations sit climber's right of the gully and off the line of ascent — skier's left as you face out on the way down — deliberately taking the descent out of the gully feature the route climbs. You reach it by downclimbing the arete's 3rd/4th-class ground plus one short, exposed 5th-class step.

rappel_detail.pull: Steep and fairly clean on a 60 m rope, provided the strands are kept out of the gully when you throw.
rappel_detail.notes: Continues down the arete; short easy downclimbing sections connect stations.
hazards: The gully immediately beside the line is the loose ground that produced the 2022 rockfall. Keep ropes and feet out of it — that is the whole reason this rappel line was moved.
This is a very popular route and stations back up on summer weekends; anything knocked loose lands on the party waiting below.
rappel_detail.station: Second of the three chain-and-bolt stations, on the ledge just above the chockstone, again set off to the side of the climbing line. Short sections of easy downclimbing link it to the station above, and how much you rappel versus downclimb is a party choice.

rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel returns to the base of the route.
hazards: Talus and slabs immediately below the last station, with the pull zone directly above anyone still coiling ropes.

The alternative descent some parties take instead — traversing to the Southwest Couloir and walking it out — avoids rope work but is loose and can hold firm snow well into summer, so it is not automatically the safer option without an axe.
rappel_detail.station: Lowest chain station. The rappel from it returns you to the base of the route, where the climbers' trail leads back down through talus and slabs alongside the stream to the Blue Lake Trail.

wa_south_early_winter_spire_direct_east_.rappel_count_note: Three rappels on a single 60 m rope, but they are not this route's own stations — the descent downclimbs the South Arete and uses the three bolt-and-chain stations North Cascade Mountain Guides installed there after the June 2022 rockfall, which are shared with the South Arete, Southwest Rib and other South Early Winters Spire routes. The South Arete descent is given as two to three rappels because the connecting ground can be downclimbed instead; three is the number of fixed stations. Per-station lengths are not known, so none is shown.

approach_variants.name: Spire Gully from the SR-20 hairpin (dry)
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the dirt pullout on the obvious hairpin turn on SR-20, directly beneath the east faces of the two Early Winters Spires. Do not use the Blue Lake Trailhead — that is the west-side approach and it puts you on the wrong side of the mountain.

Walk up the obvious gully, which is the easy way through the first band of cliffs above the road. Above that cliff band a faint climbers' path leaves the gully on a gently rising line to the right, crossing easy slabs and vegetated dirt. Roughly three quarters of an hour out you come to some fourth-class slabs.

The classic sequence of landmarks, and the one to hold in your head: up Spire Gully following occasional cairns to the last big tree in the middle of the gully; from that tree traverse right across talus; that brings you under the gully that runs up to the notch between North and South Early Winters Spires; then traverse left to the foot of the buttress.

The whole line is visible from the road, so look up and read it before you start walking.
hazards: loose rock in Spire Gully, with parties above
fourth-class slabs partway up the approach — a fall there is consequential and unroped
vegetated dirt slopes that are greasy when wet
no water on the approach
approach_variants.baseFinding: The buttress toe is the low point of the prow, sitting immediately left of the gully that separates North from South Early Winters Spire — so you find it by first locating that dividing gully and then stepping left out of it, rather than by heading straight up from the talus. The first pitch is rambling 5.6 with moss, dirt and some loose rock; a scruffy easy pitch is the correct start here, and if your first pitch is clean and steep you are too high on the buttress or on one of the harder east-side lines. The last large tree in the centre of Spire Gully is the checkpoint before this: if you are still climbing the gully and have passed no such tree, you have not reached the traverse point yet.

approach_variants.name: Early-season, snow in Spire Gully
approach_variants.notes: Same line from the hairpin, but with snow in Spire Gully the traverse right from the last big tree is done on snow rather than talus. Crampons and an axe are worth carrying; sources on this approach say so explicitly for the early season. SR-20 is gated over Washington Pass through the winter, typically from late November or early December to mid-April or early May, so this window opens with the highway.
hazards: snow traverse above a runout
moat at the base of the buttress
wet-loose slides off the east faces on a sunny spring day
SR-20 gated in winter
approach_variants.whyThisWay: From the highway opening through June, when Spire Gully still holds snow and the traverse is done on snow, with an axe and crampons for the extra firmness.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Snow does not move the buttress toe — it is still the low point of the prow just left of the North/South Early Winters dividing gully. What it changes is the traverse: on snow the rightward traverse from the last large tree in the gully is a straightforward but exposed snow crossing rather than a talus scramble, and the transition back onto rock at the base of the buttress will likely involve a moat. Fix the dividing gully visually from the highway before you start — from inside a snowy Spire Gully in flat light the individual features all read the same.

bivy.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside bivy
bivy.notes: The usual answer for a car-to-car day on this group, and the start of every west-side approach, about a mile west of Washington Pass. Parties routinely sleep at the lot or at the highway hairpin rather than walking in, because the approaches are short enough that a high camp buys little. There are no facilities and no water; it is a place to sleep in or beside the car, not a campsite. Highway 20 is closed through the winter, so this is unavailable until the road reopens.
bivy.water: None at the trailhead. Carry what you need.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park
bivy.capacity: Informal, at the parking area — no prepared sites

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground, about a ten-minute drive east down the highway from the Blue Lake trailhead, in the trees along Early Winters Creek. No reservations, so it is a gamble on a summer weekend. Its season runs roughly from late spring into autumn and is decided by snow rather than by a date.
bivy.water: Early Winters Creek runs through the campground

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground
bivy.notes: Further east and lower than Lone Fir, which means it opens earlier in the season when the higher options are still under snow — the practical choice for an early-season trip. It sits far enough off the highway to be quiet and has more plumbing than anything nearer the climbing. The trade is a longer drive to the trailhead each morning. Check current status before relying on it; the highway-corridor campgrounds take periodic maintenance closures.
bivy.water: Piped water, sinks and flush toilets

bivy.name: Liberty Bell basin dispersed sites
bivy.notes: Sites in the basin on the west side of the group, reached by following the Blue Lake trail and then the signed climbers' path that branches off it toward the group. Worth it if you want to be under the west-side routes at first light rather than walking up from the road. Note the separate restriction around Blue Lake itself, where overnight camping is not allowed within a quarter mile of the lake — the basin sites are the ones to aim for, not the lakeshore. Treat it as a basin camp below the spires rather than a fixed spot.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and seasonal runoff in the basin — unreliable once the snow has gone
bivy.permit: No permit for dispersed camping; this is national forest, not the national park

approach_variants.name: Eightmile Creek trail, South Buttress branch, then up to the terrace
approach_variants.notes: Drive and walk exactly as for the Great Arch: FR 2060 off the Mountain Loop Highway, right at the mile-5 fork, Eightmile Creek trailhead, then the Eightmile Creek trail for 30-40 minutes to the talus slope, and the climbers' branch up and left into the slide maples within about 100 feet of leaving the woods.
hazards: Unmarked brushy climbers' path through slide maple
Scrambling onto the terrace above the Great Arch
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route does not start where the approach path meets the rock. It starts from a terrace that sits between the Great Arch area and the start of The Big Tree, and the easiest way onto that terrace is from the Great Arch side.

So the sequence is: reach the Great Arch, then gain the terrace and walk along it toward the Big Tree side. If you are standing on the ground at the zig-zag crack you are at The Big Tree, not this route; if you are at the large left-facing flake with a bolt on it you are at Under the Bored Walk.

Having to scramble up onto a terrace before racking up is correct here.

approach_variants.name: East end of the pullout, downhill to the Lower Wall
approach_variants.notes: Pullout on the north side of US-2 near milepost 96.5, west of Leavenworth. From the lower, eastern end walk about fifty yards downhill to the climbers' trail, which climbs steeply to the Lower Wall base.
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
hazards: Steep climbers' trail from the road
Full southwest sun and polished rock
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Take the trail from the eastern end of the pullout, not the western one — the western trail traverses onto Logger's Ledge and serves Upper Castle, a full wall higher.

Running west to east along the Lower Wall's selected routes, the order is The Fault, Catapult, The Vertebrae, The Bone, so this is the third along. The Fault is the one the short trail from the right of the parking area reaches directly, which makes it the easiest fixed point to count from.

The wall itself is identified by its many roofs and by sitting directly under Logger's Ledge. Newer routes on the right side of this wall carry more bolts than the older ones, so an unusually well-protected line here means you have drifted east.
